naive_days_over_365.note: Strawman baseline: days/365 everywhere, ignoring the basis field entirely. Recorded to bound the floor, not as a competing method.

naive_30_360_no_eom_rules.note: NEAREST REAL COMPETITOR. 30/360 without the last-day-of-February and 31->30 cascade is the textbook 'Bond Basis' most non-specialist implementations produce, and it is a defensible reading of an under-specified 30/360 - not a strawman.

naive_actact_calendar_denom.note: REAL COMPETITOR. ACT/ACT with a plain calendar-year 365/366 denominator is the published ACT/ACT ICMA-vs-ISDA confusion; a competent analyst reaches it by applying the ICMA period rule to an ISDA instrument.

naive_isda_as_365f.note: REAL COMPETITOR. Collapsing ACT/ACT ISDA to Actual/365 Fixed is the single most common documented convention slip in fixed-income analytics.

naive_360_for_365_mixup.note: Strawman baseline: /360 where /365 is specified. Recorded to bound the floor.

method: ISDA 2006 Sec 4.16 day-count fractions: 30/360 US Bond Basis (Feb-EOM + 31->30 ordered cascade), 30E/360 (unconditional 31->30), ACT/360, ACT/365 Fixed, ACT/ACT ISDA (leap-day-splitting: days in leap years over 366 plus days in non-leap years over 365), ACT/ACT ICMA (period-based denominator = frequency * days-in-reference-period); accrued = notional * annual_coupon_rate * year_fraction
published_precision_ambiguity_note: MEASURED, not asserted. ISDA 2006 section 4.16 fully specifies every basis here - the day counts and denominators are defined exactly, so there is no rounding or tabulation ambiguity of the kind that bites a standard quoting values to N decimals. The residual spread between two faithful implementations is floating-point only: verifier/test_outputs.py::test_golden_recomputes_from_inputs re-derives every golden from the shipped dates with an independent hand implementation of the six bases and agrees with the QuantLib-baked ledger to <= 1e-12 on year_fraction. The graded tolerance is 1e-10, i.e. at least 100x that band, so no faithful reading of the convention can fail on precision.
